pois.name: Takeshita Street
pois.description: 350-metre pedestrian street — Tokyo's epicentre of Harajuku street fashion, cosplay, and youth culture since the 1980s. Peak on Sundays: over 200,000 visitors. Crepe stands, gothic-lolita boutiques, and streetwear pop-ups line every metre.

pois.name: Meiji Jingu Shrine
pois.description: Shinto shrine (1920) dedicated to Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken, set in 70 hectares of forest. The towering wooden torii gate is one of Japan's largest — 12 metres high, built from 1,500-year-old Taiwanese cypress. Sees 3 million visitors in the three days of New Year's.

pois.name: Yoyogi Park
pois.description: 54-hectare urban park, former 1964 Olympic Village. Cherry blossoms (hanami) in April draw half a million visitors. Rockabilly dancers and street musicians perform at the main gate on Sundays — a Tokyo Sunday ritual since the 1980s.

pois.name: Omotesando
pois.description: Tokyo's most prestigious shopping boulevard — a zelkova-tree-lined avenue flanked by architecturally significant flagships: Prada (Herzog & de Meuron), Louis Vuitton (Jun Aoki), Dior, and Omotesando Hills (Tadao Ando, 2006). Often called 'Tokyo's Champs-Élysées'.

pois.name: Harajuku Station
pois.description: A small wooden JR station (original 1906 building preserved) wedged between Meiji Jingu forest and Takeshita Street. One of Tokyo's most charming and historically intact station buildings — contrasting sharply with the youth-culture explosion just outside its gates.
